They rejected the impeachment effort led by Kentucky Republican Thomas Massie and backed by Democrats. stories.headline: India Launches Anti-Dumping Probe into Aluminium Extrusions, with Solar Mounting Structures in Scope
stories.title: India Launches Anti-Dumping Probe into Aluminium Extrusions, with Solar Mounting Structures in Scope
stories.summary: India's trade remedies authority has opened an anti-dumping investigation into imports of aluminium extrusion products from China, Malaysia, Vietnam and Thailand. The scope explicitly includes solar mounting structures, which could matter for the cost of solar projects across the country. The investigation covers "Aluminium Extrusion Profiles, Structures and Articles thereof" originating in or exported from the four countries. Four countries, about 90% of imports According to the notification, imports of the subject goods from China PR, Malaysia, Vietnam and Thailand increased during the period of investigation. Together, these countries accounted for about 90% of India's total imports of the product. The Authority noted prima facie evidence that the domestic industry has suffered injury. Dumped imports were found to be undercutting domestic prices, resulting in a significant decline in profitability and losses. The industry is also facing falling cash profits, lower return on capital employed and significant underutilisation of capacity. The Authority added that complete information on the impact on economic parameters is not yet available. On dumping, the Authority said the estimated margins are above de minimis. Since price and cost data from the exporting countries were not available at this stage, normal value was constructed from the cost of production of three domestic producers, adjusted for reasonable profit and selling, general and administrative expenses. For China, producers can still seek to show that market economy conditions prevail in the industry. Export prices were derived from transaction-wise import data and adjusted to an ex-factory level. Why solar developers should pay attention The product scope goes well beyond raw profiles, bars, rods and tubes. It also covers articles made predominantly from aluminium extrusions, and the list expressly names solar mounting structures , alongside heat sinks, LED and lighting profiles, industrial T-slot framing, ladders, furniture and bicycle parts. Doors, windows, curtain-wall and façade systems are also included. The Authority's reasoning is that structures and articles are made from extruded profiles through incremental processes such as cutting, machining, welding or joining, and need no additional raw material or primary process. For initiation, they have therefore been treated as part of one product under consideration. The Authority has said the scope will be examined further after comments from interested parties. For solar, this means module mounting structure suppliers, EPC companies and developers that import aluminium structures, or depend on imported extrusions, could be affected if duties are eventually recommended and imposed. Key details of the investigation Period of investigation: 1 April 2025 to 30 June 2026 (15 months). The Authority chose this longer period because the largely MSME domestic producers maintain records on a financial-year basis. Injury period: FY2022-23, FY2023-24, FY2024-25 and the period of investigation. Unit of measurement: Metric tonnes. Tariff classification: Chapter 76 items including 7604, 7608, 7610 and 7616 99 90. The Authority has said the classification is indicative only and does not bind the scope. PCN methodology: No Product Control Number methodology has been proposed at this stage. What It Means for India's Solar Push India is building solar capacity at pace toward its 2030 goal of 500 GW of non-fossil power capacity, and every project needs mounting structures, whether on rooftops, canals or utility-scale ground-mount sites. Structures are a small slice of project cost compared with modules, but they are a visible and fast-moving part of the balance of the system, where developers and EPC firms compete hard on margins. If duties are eventually imposed, the effect will depend on how much of India's demand is met by imported extrusions and structures versus domestic fabricators, and that is exactly what the investigation should bring out. There is a fair case on both sides. Domestic extruders, mostly MSMEs, say dumped imports are eroding their prices and capacity utilisation, and a healthy local extrusion base supports the "Make in India" objective across solar and other sectors. At the same time, developers operating on thin tariffs have little room to absorb higher input costs, and a duty that touches downstream structures could squeeze them or slow rooftop and small-project rollouts. The overlap with the existing duty on solar module frames adds a further layer of trade-protection to the supply chain. The key test will be whether the final scope is drawn narrowly enough to protect domestic producers without adding avoidable cost to the energy transition. Solar developers, structure makers and importers should engage with the process early, because the window to raise scope concerns is only 15 days from the intimation letters.

stories.headline: Pollution in Delhi-NCR: Sharp increase in vehicular emissions warrant urgent intervention, says SC
stories.title: Pollution in Delhi-NCR: Sharp increase in vehicular emissions warrant urgent intervention, says SC
stories.summary: New Delhi, Nov 10: The sharp increase in vehicular emissions warrant urgent intervention, the Supreme Court has said while directing the governments of Delhi and three neighbouring states to apprise it about the steps taken to prevent the entry and operation of over-age vehicles within the National Capital Region. The apex court directed the governments of Delhi, Uttar Pradesh, Rajasthan and Haryana, the Municipal Corporation of Delhi and the Delhi Police to file detailed responses indicating any further short-term and long-term measures proposed or contemplated to mitigate vehicular emissions and reduce their contribution to the deteriorating air quality in Delhi-NCR. It also directed them to file responses on measures presently in place to identify, monitor and regulate vehicles that do not conform to the prescribed emission standards, including the enforcement of Pollution Under Control (PUC) certification requirements. A bench comprising Chief Justice Surya Kant and Justices Joymalya Bagchi and V Mohana asked these authorities to apprise it about the existing regulatory framework and enforcement mechanisms governing the entry and plying of commercial and non-commercial vehicles within Delhi and the NCR, particularly those originating from neighbouring states. The top court passed the order on November 6 while hearing a suo motu case on curbing air pollution in the NCR. The bench noted that data presented before it indicated a substantial decline in incidents of stubble burning across Delhi and the states of Uttar Pradesh, Haryana and Rajasthan. “While this development is certainly laudable, the same data also brings to the fore a converse and equally pressing concern, namely, the sharp increase in issues attributable to vehicular emissions,” it said. The top court said it must be borne in mind that Delhi and NCR, by virtue of their geographical and economic interconnectedness, bear the cumulative burden of vehicular traffic originating not merely within their own boundaries but also from neighbouring states of Uttar Pradesh, Haryana and Rajasthan. “The situation is further compounded by the substantial volume of both commercial and non-commercial vehicles entering and plying within the city from different parts of the region, thereby adding to the existing vehicular emission load,” it said. “There can be little doubt that the issue warrants urgent and immediate intervention,” the bench said. It asked these authorities to apprise it about the steps taken to prevent the entry and operation of overage, end-of-life or otherwise non-compliant vehicles within the NCR. The bench also sought response on enforcement measures undertaken against violations, including the number of vehicles inspected, challaned, denied entry or otherwise proceeded against during the relevant period. It sought responses on coordination mechanisms between the authorities of Delhi and neighbouring states for regulating inter-state vehicular movement and ensuring compliance with applicable emission norms. “The respective authorities shall also indicate the specific measures proposed to strengthen the existing enforcement mechanisms, together with a time-bound roadmap for their implementation,” the bench said. It asked the states to place on record their submissions within two weeks on steps taken by them, their responses to the suggestions of the Commission for Air Quality Management (CAQM) and the amicus curiae, and any action that they independently propose to take moving forward. The bench directed the apex court registry to list the suo motu case related to vehicular emissions and pollution in Delhi-NCR on November 23. It said that suo motu cases related to conservation and enhancement of green cover, and pollution by construction activities, power plants, and other industries would be listed for hearing on November 30 and November 26 respectively. The bench said suo motu case concerning solid waste management and burning of crop residue and firecrackers would be listed on November 25. While hearing the matter on November 6, the bench had expressed serious concern over the recurring air pollution crisis in Delhi-NCR and termed vehicular emissions a major contributor to the deteriorating air quality. It had also expressed concern over “bumper-to-bumper” traffic in Delhi-NCR. The top court had highlighted the large number of vehicles plying on roads connecting Delhi with neighbouring areas, including Ghaziabad, Greater Noida, Gurugram and Faridabad. During the hearing, the Centre had informed the bench that restrictions on the entry of vehicles below BS-VI standards were being implemented, while PUC certificates were being linked to the location where vehicle checks were conducted.

stories.title: Perception That One High Court Is Better For A Particular Dispute Is Misguided : Supreme Court Transfers IP Suit From Delhi To Madras
stories.summary: "The mere existence of territorial jurisdiction in various courts cannot on its own become justification for forum shopping and cannot result in the perpetuation of notions of a hierarchy among the High Courts of this country."

article_sentences: "The mere existence of territorial jurisdiction in various courts cannot on its own become justification for forum shopping and cannot result in the perpetuation of notions of a hierarchy among the High Courts of this country."

The Supreme Court has observed that the perception that a particular High Court is better suited to adjudicate certain types of disputes, particularly intellectual property disputes, is “entirely misguided and erroneous,” cautioning against forum shopping and notions of hierarchy among High Courts.

A bench of Justice BV Nagarathna and Justice R Mahadevan made the observation while transferring a commercial suit pending before the Delhi High Court to the Madras High Court, noting that the parties to the dispute were carrying on business in neighbouring States of Karnataka and Tamil Nadu.

“While it could be true that various High Courts may have the jurisdiction to hear a particular case, especially in the case of intellectual property disputes, any perception of a particular High Court being better suited to hearing a particular type of dispute is entirely misguided and erroneous.

We also wish to highlight that, ordinarily, in a case whose respective parties, genesis and factual locus are based in a particular location, the courts of the said location would be most suited to understanding the nuances of that case.”
The Court noted that the petitioners carry on business at Chennai, while the respondents (plaintiffs) have their principal place of business at Nelmangala, Bangalore Rural District, Karnataka.

“We fail to understand as to why the respondents/plaintiffs have filed the suit before the Delhi High Court when both the parties are residing in the neighbouring States of Karnataka and Tamil Nadu and the Madras High Court also has original jurisdiction to entertain the suit.”
“We therefore, find that the petitioner has made out a case for transfer of the suit from the Delhi High Court to the Madras High Court.

We also find that the interests of justice would be served in the instant case, having regard to the fact that the parties are carrying on their respective businesses in the neighbouring States of Karnataka and Tamil Nadu and therefore for the expediency of disposal and bearing in mind all practical aspects, the Transfer Petition is liable to be allowed.”
“Accordingly, the Transfer Petition is allowed and the case viz., CS(COMM) 625/2026 on the file of the High Court of Delhi at New Delhi is transferred to the High Court of Judicature at Madras.”

stories.headline: India building capabilities for multi-domain warfare: Defence Secretary
stories.title: India building capabilities for multi-domain warfare: Defence Secretary
stories.summary: From Operation Sindoor to drone warfare, Artificial Intelligence and space security, Defence Secretary Rajesh Kumar Singh speaks to Greater Kashmir National Editor Surinder Singh Oberoi in an exclusive interview on India’s military preparedness, evolving defence capabilities, and the challenges of future warfare. Q: India has made progress under the Make in India initiative in defence production. Where does India stand today in terms of self-reliance in manufacturing modern weapons, ammunition, aircraft, warships and advanced defence systems? A: India has made substantial progress towards self-reliance in defence manufacturing under the Make in India and Atmanirbhar Bharat initiatives. Our approach is to progressively transform India from a major importer of defence equipment into a country capable of designing, developing and manufacturing modern defence platforms and technologies. Today, India has developed significant indigenous capabilities across a wide spectrum of defence manufacturing including missiles, artillery systems, ammunition, radars, electronic warfare systems, naval platforms, armoured vehicles, helicopters and combat aircraft. This transformation is not limited to the assembly of equipment. There is a growing emphasis on indigenous design, development, critical components, propulsion systems, sensors, electronics and advanced materials. The participation of the private sector, MSMEs, start-ups, defence research institutions and established public-sector defence enterprises has further strengthened this ecosystem. There has been progress across major defence sectors. In the weapons and ammunition sector, India has expanded indigenous production of artillery guns, rockets, missiles, small arms, ammunition and armoured platforms. The indigenous ammunition ecosystem has also strengthened considerably. The Indian Army has achieved approximately 91 percent self-sufficiency across 159 of its 175 ammunition variants. In the aircraft and helicopter sector, India has developed the Light Combat Aircraft (LCA) Tejas, Advanced Light Helicopter (ALH) Dhruv and Light Combat Helicopter (LCH) Prachand. Indigenous programmes are also progressing in transport aviation, engines, avionics and airborne systems. However, certain critical technologies, particularly aero-engines, remain areas of import dependence. In the warships and submarines sector, India has made considerable progress in indigenous naval shipbuilding including aircraft carriers, destroyers, frigates, corvettes and offshore patrol vessels. The commissioning of INS Vikrant demonstrated the country's ability to design and construct a major aircraft carrier domestically. However, submarine technology, propulsion, specialised sensors and certain weapon systems remain areas requiring further development. In the missiles and advanced defence systems sector, India has developed substantial indigenous capabilities in ballistic and cruise missiles, air defence systems, radars, electronic warfare, surveillance and command-and-control systems. Systems such as Akash, BrahMos (through Indo-Russian collaboration), Pinaka and various indigenous radar systems demonstrate this progress. Advanced technologies such as high-performance engines, specialised semiconductors, certain seekers and sensors and sophisticated electronic components remain important areas of focus. Q: How much of our defence equipment is still imported? A: As per the Government of India's published figures, approximately 65 percent of India's defence equipment is now manufactured domestically, compared with an earlier import dependence of approximately 65-70 percent. This represents a significant structural change in the defence manufacturing ecosystem. However, it is important to distinguish between domestic manufacturing and complete technological self-reliance. A platform may be manufactured in India while still incorporating imported engines, electronic components, sensors, specialised materials or other critical sub-systems. article_sentences: At Orient Craft’s factory in Ranchi, hundreds of women stitch dresses, shirts and children’s clothing for British retailers Next and Marks & Spencer.
Not long ago, most of Orient Craft’s output would have gone to the US.
But founder Sudhir Dhingra, 77, has cut shipments there since the US hiked tariffs, which rose to as much as 50 per cent last year, hitting orders from customers including American Eagle and Gap.
Even with duties now lower and the possibility of a trade pact, Dhingra has decided it is too much of a risk to depend so heavily on one market.
“Even if there is a deal, what is the guarantee that it will hold water?” he said.
“I don’t wish to see that sword on my head.”

Orient Craft is one of many Indian companies reconfiguring their export destinations, and their exposure to the US, in light of the tariff shock, in a move that is likely to strengthen New Delhi’s hand in its trade negotiations with Washington, and potentially reduce India’s vulnerability to US pressure over time.

Dhingra said US buyers cancelled orders or sought discounts after US President Donald Trump first announced the tariff hikes in April 2025, with some asking suppliers to absorb 25 per cent of the duty, despite manufacturers’ margins being less than 10 per cent.
Orient Craft has since moved sales to Britain, Europe and, to a lesser extent, India.
The US now accounts for less than 10 per cent of sales, down from 84 per cent before the tariffs, with annual exports of about ₹150 crore ($15.82 million).
US duties on Indian products are currently 10 per cent under Section 301, a US law allowing tariffs on imports, as well as base tariffs from 6 per cent to 12 per cent.
Gokaldas Exports, which employs more than 53,000 people and is one of India’s biggest garment exporters, is turning to Europe.

stories.headline: Fresh snowfall in Peer Ki Gali, Gurez; Mughal Road closed ahead of major snow spell in J&K
stories.title: Fresh snowfall in Peer Ki Gali, Gurez; Mughal Road closed ahead of major snow spell in J&K
stories.summary: Srinagar, Nov 11 : Fresh snowfall was reported at Peer Ki Gali along the Mughal Road and in Gurez Valley on Wednesday, prompting authorities to suspend traffic on the strategic road and restrict tourist movement in vulnerable areas ahead of a major spell of rain and snowfall forecast across Jammu and Kashmir from November 12 to 14. Officials said the Mughal Road, which connects south Kashmir with Rajouri and Poonch districts, was closed for vehicular movement following light rain and snowfall in the Peer Ki Gali area. Deputy Superintendent of Police Traffic, Rajouri-Poonch Range, Ajaz Ahmed Choudhury, said the closure was ordered as a precautionary measure due to slippery road conditions. Commuters have been advised to avoid travelling on the route until further clearance and remain in touch with traffic control rooms for updates. Gurez Valley in north Kashmir also received fresh snowfall, covering parts of the area in a white blanket, as the district administration had already advised tourists against visiting the valley in view of the impending weather conditions. The Meteorological Centre Srinagar has forecast widespread rainfall in the plains and moderate to heavy snowfall in higher reaches during the three-day period, with some mountainous areas likely to receive one to two feet of snow. Speaking to news agency Kashmir News Service (KNS) Director Meteorological Centre Srinagar, Dr Mukhtar Ahmad, said an initial Western Disturbance was bringing light precipitation over isolated higher reaches, while the main weather activity was expected to begin in the early hours of November 12 and continue till the morning of November 14. "This is a significant weather system. While rainfall will dominate in the plains, we expect moderate snowfall across tourist places, marking the season's first snowfall in Doodhpathri, Pahalgam, Gulmarg and Sonamarg," Ahmad said. He said higher reaches and mountain passes, including Peer Ki Gali, Sinthan Top, Zojila, Razdan Pass, Sadhna Top and Margan Pass, were likely to receive heavy snowfall, with accumulations of one to two feet possible at some locations. The department has also indicated a 50 per cent possibility of light snowfall or mixed precipitation over the plains of Shopian, Kulgam, Kupwara, Bandipora and adjoining areas. In view of the forecast, the Bandipora district administration has temporarily prohibited tourists from visiting Gurez Valley and asked those already staying there to plan their departure immediately in coordination with the District Control Room. Candidates scheduled to appear in the Accounts Assistant written examination on November 15 have been advised to plan their journeys in advance and reach their examination centres before weather conditions deteriorate. The administration has also advised expectant mothers living in upper reaches, whose expected dates of delivery fall within the next month, to shift to nearby hospitals to ensure timely medical assistance in case snowfall disrupts road connectivity. Residents have been urged to avoid unnecessary travel towards Gurez and other higher reaches and refrain from organising social gatherings in vulnerable areas during the forecast period. Meanwhile, the Anantnag district administration has activated its District Emergency Operation Centre round the clock to deal with weather-related emergencies and public grievances. Departments, including Public Works (R&B), Mechanical Engineering, Revenue, Flood Control, PMGSY, Urban Local Bodies, KPDCL, Jal Shakti and Health and Medical Education, have been directed to take precautionary measures and keep manpower and machinery ready. The administration has issued helpline numbers 01932-227112, 9697982527, 7780885759 and 9419091681 for public assistance. The Meteorological Department has advised tourists, travellers and transporters to plan their journeys in advance, check road conditions before setting out and strictly follow traffic advisories. Farmers have also been advised to suspend harvesting operations on November 12 and 13 and ensure that harvested crops are safely stored to prevent damage from rain and snowfall. The fresh snowfall and the approaching weather system could affect traffic on several important mountain routes, including the Srinagar-Leh highway via Zojila, the Mughal Road and other high-altitude passes, the advisory said. (KNS)

stories.headline: 1.01 lakh daily wagers await regularisation as Omar Govt’s committee misses deadline
stories.title: 1.01 lakh daily wagers await regularisation as Omar Govt’s committee misses deadline
stories.summary: Srinagar, Nov 10: More than a year and a half after constituting a high-level committee to address the long-pending regularisation of daily wagers and other temporary employees, the Omar Abdullah-led government is yet to come up with a concrete policy, leaving thousands of workers in uncertainty despite repeated assurances and an explicit electoral commitment to resolve their grievances. The committee, constituted in March 2025 under the chairmanship of the then Chief Secretary Atal Dulloo, was given six months to examine the legal, administrative and financial aspects of regularisation and recommend a comprehensive framework. However, the deadline passed without the report being submitted, and the issue remains unresolved even after the retirement of its chairman on October 31. The delay has once again brought the government's handling of the issue under scrutiny, particularly because the regularisation of daily wagers was among the commitments made by the ruling National Conference in its 2024 election manifesto. The party had promised to formulate a policy for regularisation of daily wagers, casual labourers, CIC operators, contractual employees, Home Guards, Rehbar-e-Kheel and other temporary employees in a time-bound manner. After assuming office, the government constituted the committee through Government Order No 384-JK(GAD) of 2025 dated March 19. Its mandate included examining the nature and duration of workers' engagement, their eligibility, availability of sanctioned posts, recruitment rules and the financial implications of regularisation. Despite the stipulated six-month period, the government has not made the committee's recommendations public or announced a revised deadline for completing the exercise. The delay also came under scrutiny within the ruling establishment when National Conference spokesperson and MLA Tanvir Sadiq urged the then Chief Secretary to submit the pending report before his retirement on October 31. However, the deadline passed without any publicly announced submission. With Sajjan Singh Yadav taking over as Chief Secretary on November 1, the responsibility of taking the pending exercise forward now rests with the new administrative leadership and the chief minister. The latest admission came from Minister for Rural Development and Panchayati Raj Ali Mohammad Sagar on November 1, when he acknowledged that the committee had missed its deadline, citing administrative constraints under the Union Territory framework. The government's September 29 reply in the Legislative Assembly had also indicated the uncertainty surrounding the issue, stating that no fixed timeline could be provided for regularisation because of the multiplicity of categories and the legal, administrative and financial implications involved. The response has left workers without clarity on when the committee will complete its work, when the government will take a final decision or how the proposed regularisation process will be implemented. The scale of the problem is reflected in the government's own figures. As many as 1,00,501 casual and other daily-rated workers have been registered through Aadhaar-based biometric identification and skill profiling across different government departments and institutions. Of these, 57,390 belong to Kashmir division and 40,077 to Jammu division. The registered workforce includes 69,696 casual labourers, 8534 seasonal labourers, 8836 daily-rated and work-charged employees, 3092 part-time workers, 5757 hamals and drivers associated with the Food, Civil Supplies and Consumer Affairs Department, 1929 Hospital Development Fund workers, 2153 part-time sweepers, 156 CIC operators and 348 settlement assistants in the Revenue Department. The Public Health Engineering and Irrigation and Flood Control sectors account for 38,585 workers, followed by the Power Development Department with 13,616, Education with 12,646, Forest with 8317 and Public Works (R&B) with 6801. These workers perform duties in departments responsible for essential public services, yet many continue to remain outside the regular employment structure despite years of service. The financial condition of a significant section of this workforce is equally distressing. Jammu and Kashmir Casual Daily Wagers Forum president Sajad Ahmad Parray said that monthly earnings of daily wagers range between Rs 2500 and Rs 9000, depending on their category of engagement. For workers supporting families, these earnings are increasingly inadequate to meet household expenses, children's education costs, healthcare requirements and other basic needs. The uncertainty is compounded by the age profile of the workforce. Parray has said nearly 30 percent of daily-rated employees are approaching the age of superannuation within the next six to seven months. For those who have spent 20 to 30 years working in government departments, the absence of a regularisation policy raises the prospect of reaching retirement without adequate financial security or clarity about their future. The government has not publicly outlined a separate mechanism for workers nearing retirement or clarified how the cases of those who have already retired while awaiting regularisation will be addressed. On November 3, hundreds of daily wagers affiliated with the All J&K Daily Wagers Sangharsh Samiti attempted to march towards the Civil Secretariat in Jammu, demanding regularisation and implementation of the Minimum Wages Act. In Kashmir, the Jammu and Kashmir Casual Daily Wagers Forum has also repeatedly raised the issue of the pending committee report. Parray has warned that continued neglect could force workers to intensify their agitation, including disrupting essential services, while emphasising that workers want their grievances resolved through dialogue. The government has cited legal and financial complications in framing a regularisation policy, particularly because workers belong to different categories and were engaged under different terms and conditions. Senior government officials, meanwhile, have indicated that regularisation of such a large workforce is not a straightforward administrative decision, given its substantial financial implications. They said any decision to regularise more than one lakh registered temporary workers would have long-term implications for the government's recurring expenditure, including salaries, pensions and other employee-related liabilities. A major portion of Jammu and Kashmir's annual budget is already committed to meeting salary and pension obligations, leaving limited fiscal space for additional recurring expenditure. Regularising such a large workforce would therefore require a detailed assessment of the financial burden, availability of sanctioned posts and the government's capacity to sustain the additional expenditure over the years. Officials said the government would have to proceed cautiously, keeping in view the long-term fiscal implications rather than taking a decision without examining its sustainability. However, the financial considerations also underline the need for the committee to complete its exercise and place concrete recommendations before the government. The longer the process remains inconclusive, the longer workers will remain uncertain about their future, without even knowing which categories could qualify for regularisation or when a decision may be esr xpected.
